sentences.text: The name Eocarcharia combines Greek words for 'dawn' and 'shark' to reflect its early divergence from 'shark-toothed' relatives.
The species name dinops means 'fierce-eyed' and refers to the unique ornamentation on the postorbital bone above the eye.
Eocarcharia is characterized by a robust postorbital bone with a large brow.
The position of the orbital boss above the top back edge of the orbit is a diagnostic trait unique to Eocarcharia.
Unlike Mapusaurus and Giganotosaurus, the postorbital bosses of Eocarcharia lack extensive ossification.
Eocarcharia has a narrow postorbital facet articulating with the jugal, distinguishing it from the broader facets of Carcharodontosaurus.
The dentary bone of the Eocarcharia taxon possesses 15 tooth sockets.
The teeth of the Eocarcharia taxon have transversely compressed crowns.
The fused skull bones indicate that the referred specimens were fully mature adults.
Researchers hypothesize that Eocarcharia's robust brow was covered in keratin and used for head-butting.
Researchers hypothesize that the brow of Eocarcharia was covered in keratin, which would have extended its size.
Eocarcharia was formally described in 2008 by Paul Sereno and Steve Brusatte.
The genus Eocarcharia contains only one species, Eocarcharia dinops.
The fossil collection includes a maxilla, maxilla fragments, five postorbitals, two frontals, and five teeth.
The holotype specimen of Eocarcharia is the postorbital bone cataloged as MNN-GAD2.
Sereno and Brusatte described Eocarcharia in 2008 as an early-diverging allosauroid theropod within the family Carcharodontosauridae.
Sereno and Brusatte named the genus Kryptops palaios in their 2008 paper describing Eocarcharia.
Sereno and Brusatte hypothesized that the postorbital bosses of Eocarcharia were used for intraspecific lateral head-butting.
Initially, all referred material was classified as a single species of early-diverging carcharodontosaurid.
Cau and Paterna noted that two unique traits proposed for Eocarcharia are also shared with the spinosaurid Ceratosuchops.
Cau and Paterna considered Eocarcharia to be a spinosaurid based on its similarities to Suchomimus, Ceratosuchops, and Riparovenator.
Cau and Paterna placed Eocarcharia as the sister taxon to the spinosaurid Suchomimus in their phylogenetic analysis.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Eocarcharia as Carcharodontosauridae.
The type species of the genus Eocarcharia is Eocarcharia dinops.
Eocarcharia lived in the western Ténéré Desert of Niger.
Eocarcharia fossils date to the Early Cretaceous (Aptian–Albian ages) and were found in the Elrhaz Formation at the Gadoufaoua locality.
Eocarcharia inhabited an environment of rivers and vast floodplains shared with other dinosaurs, pterosaurs, and crocodylomorphs.
Fossils of Eocarcharia have been found in the Elrhaz Formation of the Tegama Group in the Gadoufaoua area of the Nigerian Ténéré Desert.
Eocarcharia likely inhabited habitats dominated by inland floodplains or riparian zones.
Eocarcharia coexisted with theropods including the spinosaurid Suchomimus, the chimeric Kryptops, and the noasaurid Afromimus.
The fossil site of Gadoufaoua contains remains of megaherbivores such as Ouranosaurus, Lurdusaurus, Elrhazosaurus, Nigersaurus, and an unnamed titanosaur.
The time range for Eocarcharia is recorded as 121.4 to 100.5 million years ago.
Later studies suggest Eocarcharia may be a chimaera, combining bones from at least two unrelated taxa rather than a single species.
Some researchers propose that the holotype specimen belongs to a baryonychine spinosaurid closely related to Suchomimus.
Matthew Carrano and colleagues hypothesized in 2012 that the holotype of Kryptops palaios was a chimera containing postcranial bones possibly belonging to Eocarcharia.
